newsitem.title: GERMANY: Adidas confident of higher 1997 profit.
newsitem.headline: Adidas confident of higher 1997 profit.

text.p: German sportswear maker adidas AG said on Wednesday it was confident that it would report higher sales and profit for 1997 after record results in 1996 and would meet market expectations.

"All in all, we are confident that our business prospects for the full year are very favourable for ensuring further steady growth in sales and profitability, and thus living up to the expectations of our investors and the financial community," adidas chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said in the text of a speech at the group's annual general meeting.
Louis-Dreyfus said Adidas' order backlog at the end of March was indicative of the group's strength, which had risen 36 percent during the 1997 first quarter compared with the same period in 1996.
Adidas, best known for its three-stripe logo, reported a 43 percent rise in first quarter net sales to 1.7 billion marks ($998.4 million), while pre-tax profit rose 42 percent to 243 million marks.
Net sales for 1996 rose 35 percent to 4.7 billion marks, while pre-tax profit rose 50 percent to 444 million marks behind a 51 percent surge in apparel sales and a 21 percent gain in footwear sales.
The positive outlook for 1997 underpinned adidas shares in bourse trade, reaching a new record high at 191.50 marks before easing to trade up 1.50 marks to 191 marks.
Louis-Dreyfus also said adidas was interested in share buyback proposals once they become applicable under German law.
"We consider share buybacks as an interesting concept to provide shareholders with cash and at the same time potentially increase the value of the adidas share," Louis-Dreyfus said.
But he added, "We believe that our industry offers ample growth opportunities which can provide shareholders with attractive value enhancement for their funds invested."

He also defended adidas' dividend payout policy despite criticism from some German shareholder groups, saying it was in line with the policy outlined when adidas was floated in November 1995 and also with dividends of major competitors.
Adidas had proposed a 1996 net dividend of 1.10 marks per share, which was a payout ratio of 16 percent of net income.
But he hinted at the prospects for higher dividend payouts in the coming years.

"As the financial leverage in our balance sheet continues to decline, we will certainly look into the possibility to increase dividend payments, and analyse in detail other options available, to redeem shareholders and adjust our capital structure," Louis-Dreyfus said.
